The First Estonian Newspaper: In Parnu, the schoolmaster Johann Voldemar Jannsen has begun publishing Perno Postimees - the first newspaper in the Estonian tongue. Farmers read it aloud in the township houses - the words of the nation now travel faster than the manor lords can count. A national awakening is stirring.
Mu isamaa on minu arm!
It is but peasant sentiment.
Eesti Postimees and the Readers Circles

Jannsen has moved to Tallinn and founded Eesti Postimees, and with it a network of readers circles across the land. Literate farmers now write to each other, subscribe together, and organize choirs around the arriving post.
A newspaper in every township house.
The censor will have his say first.
The Kalevipoeg Is Read Aloud
Kreutzwald's epic of Kalev's son has passed from the scholars' salons to the farmhouse evenings of the land. Where the songs are sung, the idea of a nation grows.
Sing on, ye people.
A Nation of Singers

Tens of thousands have gathered on the song grounds. Choirs from every county, in national dress, singing in one voice. Foreign newspapers send their correspondents - the world takes note of a small people singing loudly.
Let the songs be heard across the Baltic!
Jakobson and the Sakala Generation

Carl Robert Jakobson has raised a fierce voice in the pages of Sakala: schools in Estonian, honest courts, and an end to Baltic German privilege. His pen stings the manor lords and excites the peasantry alike.
We shall not be mocked in our own land!
Prudence - the time is not yet ripe.
The Alexander School Movement

Across the land, farmers are collecting kopecks into a great common purse: a school of higher learning where the language of instruction shall be Estonian. The Alexander School committee gathers in Tartu to count the pennies of the poor.
Our pennies shall build our school.
Keep the money in the parish.
The Pressure of Russification

New orders arrive from Saint Petersburg: Russian in the schools, Russian in the offices, Russian in the churches of the wrong rite. The Baltic German gentry lose their privileges - the Estonian peasants lose their language.
We will keep our tongue behind closed doors.
The storm will pass - bend but do not break.
Tõnisson's Postimees

A young Tartu lawyer, Jaan Tõnisson, has taken over the daily Postimees and made it the schoolbook of the nation. His editorials call for patience, law, and organization - and for Estonians to become a nation of readers, not rebels.
A newspaper in every farmhouse.
The Vaps Movement

Veterans of the war, in uniforms too worn to surrender, march through Tallinn demanding a stronger state. They recall the subsidized grain of the war years and the corruption of the old parties. Some hail them as saviors - others hear in their boots an echo of Italy. The government must decide what to do with an army that marches on its own capital.
Their grievances are our grievances.
The republic has one army, not two.
The Armored Train Doctrine

After the war, the soomusrong regiments have been studied by our general staff. Where the rails run, an armored train is a fortress that moves. Our doctrine now builds upon rails, naval guns, and volunteer crews.
Standing orders for the Armored Train Division!
Careful maintenance wins wars.
Brothers Across the Gulf

Across the water, Finland stands free of the Tsar's grasp. Both nations claim the same songs and nearly the same words. Volunteers and rifles have already crossed the gulf in both directions - now the two governments prepare to bind their fortunes together.
One sea, two shores, one kinship.
The Coastal Swedes Petition

The old Swedish fishing villages of the coast and islands - Ruhnu, Vormsi, Noarootsi - have sent a petition to Tallinn. Their pastors ask only that their tongue may live where it has lived for seven hundred years.
Their home is our home - their rights are ours to guard.
A nation must first look to its own.
The Cultural Autonomy Law

The Riigikogu has passed a law unique in Europe: any community of three thousand souls may form its own cultural self-government, with its own schools and church affairs. Minorities need no longer fear the state - the state has made loyalty cheap and treason pointless.
Let every tongue bloom in its own garden.
The December Rising

Before dawn, shots crack through Tallinn: the communists have risen, aiming to seize Toompea and hand the country to Moscow. By morning the rising is broken - by evening the nation stands taller for having survived it.
The republic defended itself, as it always must.
The World Depression Reaches Us

The crash of foreign markets has strangled the export of butter, bacon and paper. Unemployment walks the streets of Tallinn and Narva, and the government must choose which of its promises to keep and which to break.
Ride out the storm - balance the books.
Borrow and spend - the people must eat.
The New Constitution

A draft constitution has been prepared for the state: a strong president above the parties, a chamber of national and professional interests, and the rights of the individual written plainly. Its authors call it a constitution for the Estonian character.
It shall be the law of the land.
The Ultimatum

Moscow demands naval and air bases on our soil, "for our mutual protection." The signature is demanded within hours. The armies that could defend us are an ocean of distance away - yet yielding now may only postpone what yielding invites.
Sign. Survival first.
We will not sign away our soil.
The Generals of the War

The war is won, and its commanders have become the first soldiers of the republic: Johan Laidoner, who commanded the Viru front - and Andres Larka of the armored trains. The republic pins its medals and keeps its generals close.
For honor, for the nation - and well earned.
Ernst Põdder and the Kaitseliit

Ernst Põdder is the very picture of our fighting spirit - a soldier who personally led his men through fire and kept them standing when the front seemed lost. Now he takes up the cause of the Kaitseliit, the volunteer Defence League, turning farmers and students into a citizen army sworn to the nation. A commander like this comes once in a generation.
Give him a command and the nation's trust.
The republic has enough soldiers.
Found the Armored Train Division

The armored trains that broke the Red advance were improvised by a handful of officers and volunteer crews. Now let the improvisation become an institution: a standing Armored Train Division, with workshops, rail garrisons, and a proper war flag.
Establish the Estonian Kroon
A young nation trades in borrowed coin. A currency of our own - the kroon - will let the republic price its bread in honest numbers and pay its way without a banker's leave.
Endorse the Sakala Society

Carl Robert Jakobson's newspaper Sakala has become the organ of the radical national movement, read aloud in the township houses of Viljandimaa. Endorsing the society will spread its network of reading rooms and choirs across the province.
Organize Setomaa

Beyond the lakes of the southeast live the Setos, Orthodox in faith and Estonian in loyalty, keeping their half-sung half-spoken language on both sides of the border. Bringing their hamlets under orderly administration will steady the frontier.
Found the Young Eagles
Let the boys of the republic have wings before they have rifles: a youth organization of sport, scouting and national spirit, so that the next generation grows strong in body and loyal in heart.
Expand the Defence League

The Kaitseliit proved itself in the war, but the Defence League is still a brotherhood of rifles and good intentions. Armories, drill grounds, a permanent staff and district commands will turn volunteers into a reserve the army can count.
Fortify the Narva Line

The river Narva has always been the gate of Estonia, and the gate wants a lock. Concrete positions along the east bank and depth works behind them will make the frontier a wall rather than a line on a map.
Build the Coastal Defence
Tallinn's harbor is the republic's front door and its weakest wall. Coastal batteries on Aegna and Naissaar, mine stores and signal stations will make the Gulf a door that can be barred.
Expand the Kreenholm Works

On the falls of the Narva stands the largest cotton mill in the empire, Kreenholm, with its own hospital, schools and thousands of hands. Expanding the works will make Narva an industrial city and the republic a cotton power.
Estify the University of Tartu

For three centuries the language of the lecture hall has been Latin, then German, then Russian - everything but the language of the land. From this term, the University of Dorpat becomes the University of Tartu, and the language of instruction becomes Estonian.
Found the Bank of Estonia
A state needs more than money - it needs the machinery of money. The Bank of Estonia, Eesti Pank, shall issue the kroon, guard the gold reserve, and stand behind every note the treasury prints.

The Orthodox Mission

In the villages near the Narva river and the shores of Lake Peipus, peasants have begun crossing over to the Orthodox faith. They seek the protection of the Tsar from the manor lords, and every baptism is heard in the churches and the chancelleries alike.
Faith is free - and owed protection.
The Lutheran church must stand firm.
Farms for Free Men
New land regulations allow the peasants to purchase their farms as freehold property. Across the land, families count their kopecks and dream of deeds written in their own names.
Let the land belong to those who till it.
The Telegraph Line

A humming wire now binds Tallinn to Tartu. Messages that once took two days by post coach now arrive before lunch. Merchants, officials and newspapermen alike learn to live at the speed of electricity.
The nation speaks with one wire.
The Parish School Law

Every township is now bound to keep a school and pay a teacher. In the farmhouse classrooms, children learn their letters in the mother tongue, and the bondsmen of yesterday become the readers of tomorrow.
A school for every parish.
The Kreenholm Strike
At the Kreenholm manufactury by the Narva falls, thousands of workers have downed their shuttles. They ask for shorter hours and honest pay. The strike committee waits - and so do the gendarmes.
Hear the workers out.
Send in the gendarmes.
The Temperance Crusade
Preachers of sobriety walk the parish roads, gathering thousands to sign the pledge. Behind the hymns lies a sterner promise: a sober people cannot be kept poor, or silent, forever.
Sign the pledge - awaken the people.
The vodka revenue keeps the treasury full.
Russian in the Schoolyard
Orders from Saint Petersburg now demand Russian as the language of instruction in the parish schools. Estonian children recite their lessons in a tongue their mothers do not know.
Our schools will keep the mother tongue.
The orders of the empire must be obeyed.
The Revolution in the Baltic

The news from Saint Petersburg has lit the Baltic like a spark in a rickyard. Manor houses burn in the night, workers strike in Narva and Tallinn, and crowds gather in Tartu demanding land, liberty and a say in their own affairs.
Concede the reforms - give them their say.
Restore order at any price.
The Volhynia Swedes Come Home
After two generations in the Ukraine, the Swedish families of Volhynia are returning to the coast their grandparents left. They bring ox-carts, seed grain and a dialect older than the maps.
The old villages will receive them.
There is no room on the coast.
Tõnisson’s Progress Party

Around Jaan Tõnisson and his newspaper, a new party has taken shape: patient, legal, and stubborn as field-stones. It asks for no revolution - only elections, land and schools, in the language of the people.
Organize, educate, endure.
Found the Vanemuine Society

In Tartu, the men of the awakening have founded a society for plays and song: Vanemuine, after the old god of music. Estonian words, acted by Estonians, on a stage of their own - the nation is learning to see itself.
Charter the Loan-and-Savings Societies

In the parish of Vändra, farmers have pooled their savings into a common fund, lending to one another without the manor lord or the German bank. Free men with money in their own hands are harder to turn back into bondsmen.

Darwin in the Lecture Halls

In the halls of the university at Tartu, the young naturalists are reading Darwin in smuggled copies. The rector has asked whether the Origin of Species shall be debated openly - or whether the age of authority must close its doors to the age of evidence.
Let the debate be open - truth fears no witness.
Some doors are better left closed.
The Freethinkers of Tartu

A circle of students, writers and surveyors has begun meeting above a print shop in Tartu, calling themselves the Society of Freethinkers. They publish pamphlets against superstition, and their members have quietly stopped attending church.
The age of reason has its uses.
Dissolve the society - faith is the bond of the people.
The Secular Schools Question

The township schools teach reading, arithmetic - and the catechism. A movement of teachers and parents now asks that the church lessons be set aside and the school day given wholly to useful knowledge. The pastors call it the theft of souls.
The school belongs to the nation, not the church.
Keep the catechism in the classroom.
The Quiet Congregations

In more and more parishes, the pews stand empty on Sunday mornings. Neighbors who once sang in the choir now spend the day with their books, their newspapers and their fields. The pastors ask the government to act.
Let every man keep his own conscience.
Encourage a return to the churches.
The Great Awakening

Militancy has opened a door the freethinkers did not expect: travelling preachers are filling the town squares, and thousands who had left the churches are coming back. The cabinet must choose whether to yield - or to stand firm.
Restore the ancient church of the land.
The state shall not waver.
Separate Church and State

Henceforth the state shall have no established church, and no confession shall stand above another - or above none. The congregations that remain will keep their walls and the state will keep its distance.
Sign the Concordat

After years of empty pews and silent churchyards, the state and the church have negotiated a settlement: the church returns to its ancient place in the life of the people, and the state again extends its hand to it.
The Struve Geodetic Arc

From the observatory of Tartu, the surveyors of Struve have completed a chain of triangles stretching to the very rim of the Arctic - the first accurate measurement of a meridian across an empire. The world's geographers now speak of Dorpat in the same breath as Greenwich.
Science has made our city a name in every atlas.
Koidula and the National Stage

A young poetess, Lydia Koidula, daughter of Jannsen, has given the awakening its songs and its first plays. Her verse - Mu isamaa on minu arm - sets whole song festivals weeping, and her comedies fill the Vanemuine to the rafters.
Sing, daughter of the nation, sing!
The stage is a schoolhouse - mind what it teaches.
The Old Believers of Lake Peipus

For generations the Old Believer fishermen of the Peipus shore - Varnja, Kolkja, their chapel-bells silent for two centuries - have kept their ancient rites unregistered and undisturbed. The new administration must decide whether their toleration remains the law of the land.
Their faith is their own - as it has always been.
Every soul must be counted by the church.
Truth and Justice

Across five volumes, A. H. Tammsaare has written the story of the Estonian farmer - Vargamäe's Andres and his stones, his marsh, his law. The reviews call it the novel of the people and the people call it the story of their grandfathers.
Every farmhouse shelf shall hold it.
The First Olympic Team

For the first time, a team of our own marches behind a flag of our own at the Olympic Games. The world's newspapers must spell our name correctly - and the athletes of a small nation compete for more than medals.
Send the team - let the flag be seen.
The treasury cannot afford medals.
Found the Volunteer Fire Brigades

When the church spire burns, the bucket-chain is led by farmers in brass helmets. The volunteer fire brigades of the parishes are the first schools of self-government: men who have fought a fire together have learned to trust one another with more than water.
Found the Estonian Writers' Society

In Tartu the men of the pen have formed the Eesti Kirjameeste Selts - the association of Estonian writers - to collect the folk songs, fix the spelling, and set the standards of the written word. Every grammar is a fortress.
Charter the Co-operative Creameries

The farmers of the parish have pooled their milk into the co-operative creamery: one separator, one brand, one price in the shops of London. Estonian butter shall travel under the name of the people who milked the cows.
Build the Kunda Cement Works
On the Viru coast the limestone burns day and night. A modern cement works at Kunda - the first in the land - will build the harbours, the lighthouses and the fortresses of the next fifty years.
Expand Luther's Furniture Factory

In Tallinn the Luther works has learned to peel the log into plywood - thin, strong, endless sheets of it. With new machine-halls and steam engines, Estonian furniture shall be packed in crates with the name of a small nation on every side.

Darwin in the Lecture Halls
The Tartu faculty debates Darwin and the clergy watch their flock ask harder questions.
Freethinkers Society of Tartu
Rationalist circles at the university draw clerks and artisans away from the pews.
Secular Schools
Schools run without religious instruction gently loosen old certainties.
Quiet Congregations
Neighbors keep the old forms but fewer and fewer believe.
Armored train crews drill with the army, their attached infantry hits harder and arrives in fighting shape.
The armored trains are the pride of the front, defenders hold firm knowing the Soomusrong stands with them.
Songs, newspapers and letters in the mother tongue quicken the national mind.
A shared sense of nationhood steadies the people.
The student corporations at Dorpat rival the old universities of Europe.
Evening schools carry literacy and new ideas to every parish.
Fair dealing with the Russian-speaking towns settles old grievances.
The landsturm tradition runs deep, volunteers muster quickly and willingly.
The veterans league marches in the streets, order holds, barely.
The Baltic trade accord fills Riga and Tallinn harbors alike.
The yards on the Kopli bay lay down hulls for the Baltic fleet.
A permanent staff coordinates the Kaitseliit districts.
The national epic reminds every soldier whose son he is.
Laulupidu Tradition
Finnish Nationalist Fervor
Estonian rifles and money are at work, the kindred people grow restless under the occupier.
The song festival returns every five years, a nation that sings together stands together.
The song festivals bind a nation of singers together.
The world depression bites deep, factories idle and credit dries up.
The Estonia theatre stages opera and drama in the mother tongue.
Cooperative credit frees the smallholder from the moneylender.
Parish fire brigades save towns and timber alike.
The creameries pay a fair price for every churn of butter.
Kunda cement hardens the harbors, roads and factories of the republic.
The Luther works plywood and furniture find buyers across Europe.
The Freethinkers Are Here

In the counting houses of Reval and the lecture halls of Dorpat, a small circle of educated men keeps no church. The census clerks mark them down reluctantly - the freethinkers have arrived, and they are not going away.
So there they are.
Patronize the Freethought Press
State printing contracts and lecture circuits for the unbelievers' journals: pamphlets in every parish, science in every schoolroom. Where the freethinkers are heard, the pews stand empty.
Integrate the Duchy of Lithuania

The duchy reaches south. With Vilna and Kovno in our hands, let Lithuania's crown lands be claimed for the United Baltic Duchy and its people welcomed as our own. But the Lithuanian claim does not stop at the Niemen - Memel too is an ancient Lithuanian city, and laying claim to it will not be forgotten in Berlin.
Accept the Swedish Community

For seven centuries the coastal Swedish communities have fished and traded beside us. Let them be full citizens: their language in the schools of Aiboland, their boats in our navy, their men in our councils.
The League of Militant Atheists

The revolution has its own church now: the League of the Godless, with lecture circuits where sermons used to be. The comrades demand the altars be torn from the schools and the priests' stipends given to science teachers.
The League shall have its way.
Win them with bread, not decrees.
The Minorities' Franchise Petition

With every man's vote now equal before the law, the Swedish fishermen of the coast and the German burghers of the towns have sent a joint petition to Tallinn: if our voices count at the ballot box, let our tongues and our churches count in the nation. The old estates warn of division, the new parties court them eagerly.
The franchise belongs to all who live here
A petition is not a policy
Rifles Across the Gulf,

Across the gulf, Finland groans under a foreign yoke - her language suppressed, her newspapers censored. Now men in Stockholm and Tampere ask Tallinn for money, rifles and volunteers. Helping them would strike a blow for the cause of small nations and win us glory among the awakened peoples of Europe. But the empire that rules Helsinki would notice, and it would not forgive.,
The cause of nations knows no borders,
A Knock at the Door,

The tollbooks of the Baltic ports tell their own story. Peasants from the inner governorates of the Russian Empire, hearing of wages paid in hard currency and homesteads on free land, arrive at Narva and Reval with their families and their few possessions. The Russian Empire may lose thousands of subjects a year to the New World, but more and more of them are instead choosing the shorter road west, to Estonia.,
Let them come,
Not our fight,
Estonia for Estonians - close the border,
Settlers arrive from the inner provinces of the empire, drawn by Baltic wages and Baltic schools.
The Late Awakening

The newspapers were never really stopped - they simply moved to the farmhouse evenings and the township houses, read aloud by lantern light. A movement scolded as peasant sentiment has kept its own accounts, and now the reading circles are ready to say aloud what was only whispered. The awakening arrives late, but it arrives harder.
Let it be said aloud, then.
There is no movement - keep the ledger closed.
The Coastal Swedes Remember

War has come, and the old fishing villages of the coast and islands have not forgotten the republic that guarded their tongue. From Ruhnu to Noarootsi the parish elders call the young men to the colours of the Kaitseliit - not as strangers granted leave to stay, but as sons of the land. The Defence League musters stronger than its rolls alone would suggest.
The shore people stand with us - as they always have.
Stockholm Writes Again

Years have passed, and the council in Stockholm has had time to reread the refusal. The new note is longer than the old proposal, and humbler with it: no union, no crown - a treaty of equals, trade and friendship across the gulf, each nation under its own flag. The same shores that said no to one crown may now say yes to another kind of agreement.
A treaty of equals - sign it, and let the gulf bind rather than divide.
We will keep our own counsel, as ever.
